question: A procurement officer needs a supplier comparison that must fit on one page and must not name any supplier outside the approved shortlist. Where do these two limits belong?
options: A) After the first draft arrives, so the comparison is not narrowed before she has seen the full range of options.
B) In the original request, since both limits change what belongs in the comparison, not merely how it is presented.
C) In neither place, since limits of this kind are best handled by trimming and correcting the draft she gets back.
D) Only the page limit belongs in the request; the shortlist restriction is simpler to apply while editing the draft.
correct_answers: B) In the original request, since both limits change what belongs in the comparison, not merely how it is presented.
explanations: Seeing the wider market may be useful for her own understanding, but it is a separate task. Applied here it produces a draft that has to be rebuilt around a different set of suppliers.
Correct. Both constraints determine which suppliers are compared and how much can be said about each, so stating them up front shapes the analysis instead of leaving her to reconstruct it by hand.
Trimming to one page after the fact means deciding what to cut without the original weighting, and the shortlist rule is not a trimming problem at all.
Splitting the limits leaves the harder one to manual editing, and removing an off-shortlist supplier from a comparison changes the surrounding analysis rather than a single line.
